I think we can either merge this now, and then talk about whether to remove the commit() method; or we can just go ahead and remove the commit() method in this PR. Unless someone stops by to object, I think it's up to you @Kaiido. My editor's judgement is that at this time commit() does not belong in the spec, given the signals we've seen so far.

Let me know if you want to merge this and work on commit() removal separately, or use this PR to do it all at once.

Let's do it here then. I'll update the first comment to reflect this. 

Also, it would be great if someone from Firefox and from WebKit could chime in since they do have implementations now. Based on https://github.com/web-platform-tests/interop/issues/344 I guess it's fine but if @nt1m and @zcorpan could confirm I'd feel better.

I'll open the various implementation bugs and MDN PR after said confirmation.

I think this should get two vendor support before removing.

@smfr @mattwoodrow Can you review the alternative proposal in #3677 ?

> I think this should get two vendor support before removing.

Totally agreed, thanks for the additional *cc*s.

> @smfr @mattwoodrow Can you review the alternative proposal in #3677 ?

To be clear, the status **before this PR** is:
 - According to the (broken) specs:
   - In various places, it is implied that only `.commit()` is able to update a placeholder canvas's content (a `<canvas>` on which `transferControlToOffscreen()` has been called) , even though there is also an *update the rendering* step for workers, which currently does nothing w.r.t. placeholder canvases.
   - While HTML defines only the method for the `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D`, [it states](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#the-offscreencanvas-interface:offscreencontext-commit) "*All rendering context types that can be created by an [OffscreenCanvas](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#offscreencanvas) object must implement a [commit()](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#offscreencontext-commit) method.*". No other specs (WebGL, WebGPU, etc.) has defined such a method, there is even strong signal they don't want to do so.
    - The tests for `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D#commit()` have been removed in https://github.com/web-platform-tests/interop/issues/344.
    
 - In Chrome:
   - `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D#commit()` is hidden behind a flag.
   - No other context type has the `commit()` method, not even behind a flag.
   - Update through *update the rendering* is implemented.

 - In Gecko and WebKit:
   - `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D#commit()` is implemented.
   - No other context type has the `commit()` method, not even behind a flag.
   - Update through *update the rendering* is implemented.

**After this PR**, update through *update the rendering* is the only remaining way to update the placeholder canvas content.

There is actually a few edge-cases where this might be problematic, like when the worker is killed before the next rendering update, but they can certainly be handled separately later on if needed.

Thanks for tackling this @Kaiido. We will also need a test for testing it's not supported. I would add something equivalent to https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/master/html/dom/historical.html to `html/canvas` covering this method (and any others you can think of).

I've actually wanted to add commit() to HTMLCanvasElement as well, so I don't necessarily want to remove it from OffscreenCanvas.
It's useful for being able to indicate early that an app is done rendering so that pre-painting steps can happen early, making it easier to reliably hit frame time windows.
It could also enable lower-overhead sub-RAF-rate rendering.

On the WebGL side, there is cleanup work (resolving multisampling, copying to a shared gpu resource, and/or filling the alpha channel with ones) that we do after we know a frame is done, but before we send it to the Painter. The earlier these are enqueued in the frame window, the more likely a frame is going to be complete and land within the window instead of spilling past vsync and dropping a frame.

I can only speak about the 2D context side, but I'm relatively surprised there is still an use case for `.commit()` there.  
This method is supposed to affect when the *placeholder* `<canvas>`'s content is updated, the one that's supposed to be used only to "present" the canvas content on the screen. So what this method really affects is:

 1. What content is presented on the screen.
 2. What content is used when calling `placeholder.toBlob()`, `placeholder.toDataURL()`, and when consumed by another API, like e.g. `createImageBitmap(placeholder)`.
 3. What content is fed to the streams gotten by `placeholder.captureStream()`.  

Both 1. and 3. are anyway tied to the screen refresh rate, so calling `ctx2d.commit()` won't change anything to these compared to let the *update the rendering*  steps take care of it.  
For 2. I guess sub-rAF-rate rendering could make for a potential argument, but there is already `OffscreenCanvas.convertToBlob()` and `OffscreenCanvas.transferToImageBitmap()` that can cover this use case and that seem like a better place for devs to handle it. After all, if they have a placeholder canvas it's because they have an `OffscreenCanvas` and it probably lives in another context, which means there is certainly asynchronocity between the drawing calls to the context and the calls using the placeholder content.
And since `inDOMCanvas.toBlob()` or `createImageBitmap(inDOMCanvas)` already force a synchronous update of  the canvas content, this method wouldn't do anything visible for "in DOM" 2D contexts.  

So far only the `OffscreenCanvasContext2D` version got implemented, so I guess removing it as part of this PR means that only the 2D context version would be somehow "banned" from being used anymore. If such a method is useful for other context types, wouldn't it be best for these to define it only for them instead of forcing this method on every possible future context type? I mean, per current texts even `OffscreenCanvas.getContext("bitmaprenderer")`  is supposed to have a `.commit()` method, what use case could that ever serve? And if it's supposed to do something else than update the placeholder canvas on a 2D context, maybe another method could be defined? As far as I understand it, your use case is to allow the author to tell the UA that they're done drawing on the canvas and that it can be presented as-is. If so, I can imagine a method like `ctx.lockFrame()` which could even prevent new drawings to be commited until the canvas is presented, or maybe something completely different like a `PaintController` interface or something else. But the current `.commit()` as currently defined doesn't seem to fit the bill.

The original intent of `commit()` was to address the transferred OffscreenCanvas case when OffscreenCanvas was first being designed, as @Kaiido pointed out. Eventually, we solved this with RAF on Workers. 

I get that we eventually could want to have a solution for sub-RAF-rate rendering, as Kelsey mentioned [here](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/9979#issuecomment-1845716597), but I'd argue that this would be a separate functionality from what this originally was intended for (even if we could still call this `commit()`). I think the best way to move forward would be to delete it for now and maybe start that other discussion in parallel.

Could we please unblock and land this PR?

https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/canvas.html#the-offscreencanvas-interface currently provides incorrect guidance in the second paragraph of the OffscreenCanvas specification. `requestAnimationFrame` on workers is the current cross-browser mechanism for implicit presentation to an OffscreenCanvas with any context type, both on the main thread and on web workers. While I appreciate the fact that there are use cases for presenting more manually or earlier in the frame cycle, there is currently no intent to implement `commit` in a more widespread fashion. In my opinion the HTML specification should be updated to follow past decisions and what browsers already implement.

The current HTML spec text is causing ongoing confusion among browser vendors as in https://github.com/KhronosGroup/WebGL/issues/3638 .

> Could we please unblock and land this PR?

My understanding is that this PR is opposed by two implementers, who implement `commit()`. Although the guidance might be incorrect for users of Chromium browsers, it's correct for 2/3 implementations of the web platform, so we shouldn't be modifying the HTML Standard.

Do you understand differently?

> My understanding is that this PR is opposed by two implementers

As far as I can tell only Gecko's team has expressed opposition thus far, I don't think WebKit has voiced anything yet (apart from asking to wait for 2 implementers interest and asking to review something that's been in the specs for years and is implemented everywhere).  

> who implement commit().  

No implementer has implemented what the specs are asking for. All there is now in both Gecko and WebKit is `OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D#commit()`, i.e., the version that goes on the 2D context. The specs are asking that this method is implemented on **all** the context types that are created from an OffscreenCanvas. This includes WebGL contexts (which is what brought Ken's back here I think), but also WebGPU, while [it's been voiced it's not something they want](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3872#issuecomment-1405856868), and even bitmap-renderer...

And once again, all the arguments in favor of keeping that method tend to prove that even implementers don't quite understand its purpose, which wouldn't help in the use cases that have been provided, and which is indeed obsolete since #3677. Ken is right, the text in that paragraph is wrong since the Worker's  *update the rendering* steps is now where the placeholder's content gets updated. So even if we kept the `commit()` method, the bitmap wouldn't be pushed *only* by calling it. So the specs need to be fixed anyway, better do it correctly.

Thanks for explaining. I'm unsure how to proceed here though, in light of Gecko's opposition and WebKit's lack of engagement. (I assumed WebKit would be opposed since they implement the method and removing things which their users might be relying on is risky, but I admit that was an assumption.)

Perhaps the WebGPU community, where I believe all three engines are present, can provide suggestions. Or, if you think you could create a version of this PR which sidesteps Gecko's objection and doesn't remove any methods implemented in 2/3 browsers, then we could more easily merge this without needing implementer engagement.

I discussed this with colleagues and we are very much in favor of removal and will likely remove the method from WebKit (as Chromium doesn't ship it). In particular because it completely goes against the "update the rendering" model we have today.

It's a bit unclear what to do when there's only a single implementation of a feature. I think in the past we have removed such features even when there were objections, e.g., #192.
FWIW, neither Safari nor Firefox pass [a simple test on the main thread](https://jsfiddle.net/601mwLbz/), and  I get flaky results [when a Worker is involved](https://jsfiddle.net/5hvLpr1q/).

Thanks for the updates both. From my perspective, if we can get the method removed from WebKit, then it becomes easy to remove it; a single-vendor feature with no positive signals from the other two definitely does not belong in the spec. In the current state, it's a bit more iffy, since even if WebKit supports removal, I'm hesitant to remove something that works in 2/3 browsers. @annevk, do you think removal from WebKit is imminent enough that we could just wait for that to go through?

It's tolerable to remove this, though it would be nice if the wording was not "which has become obsolete since https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3677" but instead more nuanced and accurate to consensus like "which is no longer strictly necessary since https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3677".
While we do suspect that there may be value in an explicit .commit, we can investigate that later, and when prioritization gives us time.

> It's tolerable to remove this, though it would be nice if the wording was not "which has become obsolete since #3677" but instead more nuanced and accurate to consensus like "which is no longer strictly necessary since #3677".

I reworded the initial comment, trying to keep the idea that it might actually conflict with the other rAF model, does it read better to you?
Yes, thanks!

I do not fully understand the scope of this problem, but I'd just like to chime in with some perspective as someone actively trying to port a relatively complex Wasm game engine (Bevy) to use `SharedArrayBuffers` and Web Workers.

Many native engines block their main thread for all sorts of reasons, but due to the lack of ability to block the main thread in the browser it's been recommended that Wasm engines move towards an architecture where the browser's main thread issues input events to a worker that runs most of the engine logic.

To minimize impact on Bevy users and Bevy library authors I'm trying to change Bevy's API as little as possible, and in pursuit of that I'm trying to use`OffscreenCanvas` to keep rendering logic and engine logic on the same "thread".

The simplest way I've found to approach that is to have an engine worker with an `OffscreenCanvas` that waits, using Wasm atomics, for input events sent from the browser's main thread, looping indefinitely.

The problem here is that to use the `OffscreenCanvas` properly (in the absence of `commit`) `requestAnimationFrame` must be used which means that the engine worker thread must return so that it can respond to `requestAnimationFrame` calls. This means that it cannot use Wasm atomics to wait on input events and must rely on `postMessage` which I understand to have more overhead and uncertainty in timing.

I'm still puzzling through this, so there may be something I'm missing here.

Hi @kettle11 - probably best discussed in a new issue rather than a comment on this PR, which has already been merged. Our teammate @greggman wrote [an article](https://games.greggman.com/game/offscreencanvas-and-commit/) a few years ago which describes the problems with a run-forever loop on a web worker. Additionally, @kainino0x worked with colleagues from Epic Games on their [HTML export path](https://github.com/UnrealEngineHTML5/Documentation) before it was deprecated. He prototyped the ability to manually run the browser's event loop for one step inside the run-forever loop; it doesn't work, because it causes reentrancy in unexpected ways inside both the application and the browser.

In brief, it's not difficult to refactor such C/C++ code to run its main loop one step from within `requestAnimationFrame` on a web worker, and this is the recommended strategy.
